en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
O Lord, even Brahmā, Śiva, the King of Serpents, and others do not know the limit of Your greatness even today; alas, how then could one of ignorant and fickle mind truly understand it?
Nevertheless, for the sake of purifying my own speech regarding the Lotus-Eyed One, I shall speak even a little, according to my own intellect. (1)
Some call You Brahman, others Puruṣa, and still others Karma; some call You the Buddha, others Śiva, and others the Creator (Dhātṛ).
Likewise, some wise ones call You Śakti, Gaṇapati, or the Sun. Indeed, due to the diversity of their thoughts, You are all of these; such is my conviction. 2.
Śiva has respectfully borne Your lotus-feet upon his head, and Śakti likewise possesses a body composed of the splendor of Your form;
they say that the Sun is indeed Your eye, and by these rules [of devotion], who else in this world could possibly be meditated upon as God? Tell me, O All-pervading Lord! (3)

In one place you are a fish, in another a tortoise, elsewhere a boar, and in another Narasimha; in one place you are the dwarf, as Rama the son of Dasharatha, and as the son of Nanda; in another you are Buddha and Kalki.
You roam about to remove the heavy burden of the earth; though you are independent, unborn, eternal, and all-pervading, this world is your playground. 4.
Having heard this supreme hymn uttered according to the secret tradition (Hṛdayāmnāya), Viṣṇu swiftly assumed the form of a Fish;
then, having destroyed the undecaying demon Śaṅkha, he rescued the entire collection of the Vedas from the ocean and likewise preserved the entire world which has the Veda as its sole refuge. || 5 ||

Beholding the lordly mountain suddenly sinking into the ocean, O Unconquered One, you assumed the form of a tortoise and sportively supported that deep mass of waters upon your back for the sake of the gods; was the weight of that mountain easy to bear for you, the Sustainer of the World? (6)

The asura Hiraṇyākṣa entered the ocean, the abode of crocodiles, having seized the earth; yet, while being praised by the immortals headed by Brahmā who stood in the sky, O Infinite-Souled One, this entire earth shone forth not long after it was held by you upon the tip of your tusk like a ball. (7)

O Bhūman, when asked by the lord of the Danujas, "Where is Hari?", you filled the entire world with roars and, leaping up from the pillar with your body as a man-lion, tore apart that pre-eminent Asura with your claws; was your omnipresence not thus proclaimed in the world? (8)
Beholding the goat at the doorway, though he had been forbidden by the preceptor of the Asuras, the enemy of the gods nevertheless gave him his entire body.
O Lord of the Immortals, it is well known that you are subservient to your devotees; for even now, you do not abandon the abode of Bali because of his devotion.

O Viṣṇu, having seen your father—intent on meditation—slain by the arrows of the princes, you took up your exceedingly heavy axe in rage and repeatedly cleared the entire surface of the earth of the Kṣatriyas; was your skill in removing the burden of the world not known to you? (10)
Having propitiated Umā’s Lord, he brought this entire triple world, headed by Indra, under his control; O wielder of the discus, that Lord of Laṅkā disregarded this world incessantly.
Now, before long, he has come within the range of your arrows. O enemy of the Asuras, who has not obtained the fruit of their insolence from you?
In one instance divine heroism, and in another cowardice on the battlefield; in one instance knowledge of the Gītā, and in another wandering among the wives of others;
in one instance eating earth, and in another the splendor of Vaikuṇṭha—O Giver of Refuge, your life-story is surely for the purpose of deluding those of dull intellect. 12.
The statement "one should not kill" is indeed certain and unerring; however, the phrase "the animal for Agni and Soma" has been uttered by the Brahmins.
This [latter] teaching of yours is misplaced, intended to delude the hosts of Asuras; for the prosperity of the base leads only to the suffering of the world. 13.
When the classification of the social orders and the collection of the Vedas have vanished from the surface of the earth, he will be born in a preeminent brahmin family in the city of Śambhala.
At the end of the Kali Yuga, O Lord of the Age, mounting his own horse with a glittering sword in hand, he will indeed slay the intoxicated hordes of Mlecchas.
O Giver of Fearlessness, as he sank in the deep lake, his feet dragged by the wretched water-dweller and rendered powerless in battle, he thought:
"When the Lord of Nagas, having been instantly freed from the noose around his foot, went to heaven—what then can a mere man be to you, the abode of calamities? (15)
When questioned by his sons, the Creator, being unable to provide an answer, then sought refuge in you, the Self of the three worlds.
Thereupon, their fear vanished and they attained joy; for was it not through you in the form of a swan that omniscience was proclaimed here to the Lord of the Immortals? (16)
Pierced by the arrows of his mother’s words, Dhruva went swiftly to the forest and performed supreme austerity for your ultimate satisfaction.
Even at a tender age, he attained the divine and immovable station; O Giver of Boons, when you are pleased, what in this world is difficult to obtain? (17)
Fearing the wolf, the demon Paśupati quickly broke through the fear of his own kin and, wandering through all the worlds, sought refuge with you;
yet he himself was reduced to ashes because his mind was provoked by the failure of your word. O Lord of Ramā, alas, your illusory power (māyā) is difficult for all people to fathom! 18.
Seeing the jar of nectar stolen by the invincible Daityas, you caused them to fall into delusion with side-glances through the guise of excellent young women;
O fortunate one, as you bestowed the entire ambrosia upon the hosts of gods, it seems your delight was indeed primarily directed toward your servants. (19)
Draupadī, dragged into the assembly by the wicked and finding no refuge, has cried out for your protection, O Soul of All.
Before the eyes of everyone, she has in an instant become a mass of rags; was this not the fruit of your remembrance, brought directly before our very eyes, O Blessed One? (20)

Some say your abode, O Giver of Boons, is Vaikuṇṭha; others, the world of cows (Goloka); still others, the netherworld (Pātāla) which is the dwelling place of the serpent-king; likewise, some say it is the Ocean of Milk, and others even the lotus of the heart of the virtuous. But I do not consider any of those to be your true abode, O All-pervading Lord, unless you yourself are present there. 21.

"I am Śiva among the Rudras, I am the king of the immortals among the gods, I am Vyāsa among the sages, O best of deities, I am the ocean among bodies of water, and I am Kubera among the Yakṣas"—such are your words, which I, of dull intellect, do not understand; for indeed, O Blessed One, there is nothing in this world that you are not. (22)
The sky is Your head, the moon and sun are Your eyes, the atmosphere is Your chest, and the directions are Your ears; Your speech is the multitude of Vedas, and the earth is Your waist.
The ocean is Your bladder, and the netherworld is indeed Your feet. Fools of wicked intellect, failing to recognize this true nature of Yours, despise You in human form. (23)
Your body is Vaikuṇṭha; the lotus of Your heart is the abode of Your residence; the activity of the mind is Garuḍa; and this intellect is the daughter of the ocean.

Your pastimes are the three states of consciousness, and Your vital breaths are the hosts of attendants. Alas, the multitude of people here goes outside without knowing You, failing to perceive You. 24.

O Lord, having offered his single, stainless lotus-heart to you for the sake of flowers, a person who is thus commanded quickly enters a most terrible wilderness, a dense lake, or suddenly ascends a high mountain peak; alas, such a person finds no happiness at all. (25)

O sinless one, if those who dwell in solitude, whose every hope has vanished, who are devoted to tranquility, who have mastered their inhalation and exhalation, whose bonds of worldly existence are severed, and who are well-restrained, behold the supreme light—let them indeed behold it; but let your body, embraced by my splendor, become the object of their vision. (26)

When, dwelling on the pure sands of the lofty, stainless waves of the Gaṅgā, shall I—freed from the noose of desire and escaped from the hopes of all wicked men—spend my time, O best of immortals, muttering, "O beloved of Lakṣmī, O lotus-eyed one, O Father, O Lord of the Gods, be gracious"? 27.

When shall I, dwelling upon the vast snowy mountain—abounding in peaks, surrounded by hosts of sages, covered with trees, cool, and echoing with the sweet songs of the gods—be intent on meditation in some place, utterly detached from sense-objects, and remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, the destroyer of worldly existence, attain dissolution? (28)

O Slayer of Madhu, neither the drinking of nectar, nor vast charity, nor trade, nor sacrifice, nor yoga, nor the renunciation of all enjoyments; neither chanting, nor pilgrimage, nor fierce vows—none of these are sufficient to destroy the fear of worldly existence without devotion to You. (29)
Salutations to You who are desired by all and perceived at the pinnacle of the Vedas; salutations, salutations to You who are unattached yet reside within the three worlds.
Salutations to You who are manifest and touched by the *praṇava*; salutations to You, O Soul of All! Again and again, my salutations to You. (30)

A person skilled in counting might quickly count the drops of rain from the sky, as well as the remaining grains of dust upon the earth; indeed, one might even solidify the atmosphere like leather. Yet, even so, that Lord is not able to enumerate all of Your virtues. (31)
Where is Your majesty, O Lord—which transcends all limits and lies beyond the reach of Vedic words—and where is this mind of mine, struck down by manifold afflictions?
Whatever little I have uttered here out of childishness, O Teacher, please accept it as offered with purity; for the great should not reject what is thus presented. (32)
Thus, may this most captivating hymn of praise to Hari, uttered by the paramahaṃsa sages—a locus of easily understood, beautiful, and essential words—be for the constant delight of Hari. 33.

May this supreme hymn consisting of [the names of] weapons bring auspiciousness to us—the hymn of Hari, who bears the mace, the discus, the lotus, and the conch; whose body is embraced by Ramā; and who reclines upon the body of the Lord of the Serpents. (34)

The man who, with a concentrated mind, recites this supreme hymn—which is like a dense tempest shattering the flood of worldly currents—attains here all the riches of enjoyments and is thereafter certainly glorified in the abode of Viṣṇu. (35)
Thus ends the hymn to the Greatness of Śrī Viṣṇu, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Svāmī Brahmananda.
